# Every rank-two three-cap cover has the overlap bound

This note extends the scope, not the constant, of
`candidate e239a5fb0d0efe4d`.

## Theorem

Let K be a convex body in R^d, d>=2, and let H_1,H_2,H_3 be closed
halfspaces covering K. Suppose their normals span a subspace of dimension
at most two. Write A_i=vol_d(K intersect H_i), V=vol_d(K), and use the
constants r_d from the cited source. Then

    A_1+A_2+A_3-V >= r_d min_i A_i.                       (1)

Thus every cover of a planar convex body by three closed halfplanes obeys
(1), with the sharp coefficient r_2=3/4. The covering halfplanes need not
cover the whole plane, have a positive normal dependence, or have concurrent
boundaries. For higher-dimensional K the restriction on the span of the
normals remains essential to this proof.

## A separation lemma for halfplane covers

Let D be a planar convex body and let H_1,...,H_m be closed halfplanes
covering D. If their union is not the entire plane, then two of them cover D.

To prove this, write H_i={x:u_i.x>=b_i}. The common strict complement

    Q={x:u_i.x<b_i for all i}

is a nonempty open convex set disjoint from D. The separation theorem gives
a nonzero v and a number beta such that

    v.x>=beta>=v.q  for all x in D and q in Q.

The closure of Q is P={x:u_i.x<=b_i for all i}. Indeed, fix q in Q and mix
it with any point in the latter closed intersection; all proper mixtures
are in Q and tend to that point. In particular P is full-dimensional and
v has finite supremum h<=beta on P.

That supremum is attained. Here is a direct planar verification of this
elementary polyhedral fact. Choose coordinates so v.x is the first
coordinate s. The inequalities with a nonzero second-coordinate coefficient
give finitely many affine lower and upper bounds on the second coordinate t;
the other inequalities constrain s alone. At a sequence s tending to h,
the maximum of the lower bounds is at most the minimum of the upper bounds.
These finite maxima and minima are continuous in s. At s=h the inequality
still holds. If one family is empty there is only a one-sided bound and a
finite feasible t can still be chosen; if both are empty choose t=0. The
inequalities constraining s alone also hold at h. Thus some x_0 in P has
v.x_0=h.

Let I be the inequalities active at x_0. The vector v is in the cone
generated by the active u_i. For otherwise separation from that closed
finitely generated cone gives a vector w with v.w>0 and u_i.w<=0 for
i in I. For small positive epsilon, x_0+epsilon w still satisfies the
inactive inequalities, which have strict slack, as well as all active
ones. This contradicts the maximality of x_0.

Every vector in a cone in a plane is a nonnegative combination of at most
two of its generators. One direct proof starts with any nonnegative
combination; if more than two nonzero coefficients remain, their vectors
are linearly dependent. Subtract a suitable signed dependence, choosing
its sign so it has a positive coefficient, until one coefficient becomes
zero while none becomes negative. Repeat. Therefore there are at most
two active indices J and coefficients lambda_i>=0, not all zero, with

    v=sum_(i in J) lambda_i u_i,
    h=sum_(i in J) lambda_i b_i.

If x is outside every H_i for i in J, then v.x<h. This is impossible for
x in D, since v.x>=beta>=h. Consequently those at most two halfplanes
cover D. This proves the lemma with closed covers, including tangency.

## Proof of the theorem

Project K orthogonally onto the span E of the normals. If its dimension is
one, the projected body is an interval and a finite halfline cover has a
subcover of at most two: keep the most extensive initial and terminal
halflines. Thus two original caps cover K.

Now suppose dim E=2, and let D be the projected planar convex body. If the
three projected halfplanes do not cover the plane, the preceding lemma
again gives a two-cap subcover of K. In either case, if H_j and H_k cover K
and i is the remaining index, then

    sum_l A_l-r_d min_l A_l
      >=V+A_i-r_d min_l A_l >=V,

because 0<r_d<1.

It remains to consider three halfplanes covering the whole plane. If a pair
already covers the plane we are done. Otherwise their unit normals have 0
in the interior of their convex hull. Indeed, if 0 is outside their convex
hull, strict separation gives a direction whose large negative multiples
are outside all three halfplanes. If 0 is on its boundary, the nonzero
normals on a supporting line through 0 include an opposite pair. Since
that pair does not cover the plane, its common strict complement is a
nonempty open strip. If the third normal is not parallel, movement along
this strip in one direction makes the third inequality false, contradicting
plane coverage. If it is parallel, all normals have rank one, already
handled. Therefore 0 is interior, and the three normals form a strictly
positive rank-two circuit.

The principal theorem in the cited source now applies and gives (1).
Sharpness in the planar case is the same triangle-centroid triple as there.
No alteration of cap masses or original halfspaces was made in this
reduction. In particular no boundary mass has been discarded.

## Scope of the mixed-fiber consequence

Section 6 of the cited source may consequently replace its per-fiber
positive-circuit and whole-plane-cover hypotheses by the following simpler
condition: the three actual restricted caps cover the owned fiber, and
their restricted normals span at most two dimensions. For full planar
fibers, every three-cap cover meets this condition automatically. The
case of a zero restricted normal is also included: its trace on the fiber
is either the whole fiber or the empty set. A whole trace gives a one-cap
subcover; an empty trace leaves a two-cap subcover because the original
triple covers. The elementary two-cap estimate above applies in both
cases, including rank zero. Thus no normalization by a vanishing restricted
normal is needed.

The resulting accounting inequality and its still-unproved cross-capture credit
are unchanged. There is no assertion here about groups of four or more
caps of rank three or larger, or about the sign of that credit.
